idiom_name: reader count + active-writer flag + writer-preference queue over a mutex/condition pair
implementation_notes: Classic language-neutral structure: keep an integer reader count, a boolean active writer and, for a write-preferring policy, a count of waiting writers; guard all of it with one mutex and park waiters on condition variable(s). Read acquisition waits while a writer is active or (write-preferring) writers are waiting, then increments the count; write acquisition waits until the count is zero and no writer is active; release decrements the count and wakes a writer when the last reader leaves, or clears the flag and wakes the appropriate side on write release. Always re-check the predicate in a loop after waking, because notifies may be spurious or meant for the other side. Where the runtime ships a reader-writer primitive (pthreads, POSIX pthread_rwlock_t, C++ std::shared_mutex) prefer it over hand-rolled code. Phase-fair implementations (Brandenburg & Anderson 2009) alternate reader and writer phases and provide O(1) read blocking — consider for real-time or high-contention workloads.
code_sketch:
# read
lock(gate)
while writer_active or waiting_writers > 0: wait(readers_cv)
readers += 1; unlock(gate)
... read shared state ...
lock(gate); readers -= 1
if readers == 0: signal(writers_cv); unlock(gate)
# write: wait while writer_active or readers > 0, set writer_active,
#        mutate, then clear it and notify_all - same gate, other condition
pitfalls: Waking without a predicate re-check: a spurious or wrong-side notification then either lets a caller proceed unsafely or loses a wakeup.
Waking a writer only when the reader count drops to zero, but never when a waiting writer's other conditions hold; waiters can remain parked forever.
No deliberate priority policy: a read-preferring loop starves writers under constant read traffic.
Hand-rolling without a re-check loop after a wait — one missed wakeup or spurious notify silently breaks the invariant.
Forgetting that condition variables do not remember the predicate: the loop must re-evaluate on every wake-up, even the one you just caused.
Cache-line bouncing on the reader-count word under high multi-core read contention — the lock itself becomes the bottleneck. Use per-CPU sharded variants or RCU for extreme read scalability.

Wrong move: assume a reader-preferring default is fair -> a continuous reader stream can starve a waiting writer and delay refreshes indefinitely -> instead choose and document a writer-preferring or phase-fair policy, then measure tail latency.

Wrong move: acquire a write lock while still holding a read lock -> two readers attempting the same upgrade can wait on each other forever -> instead release, acquire, and re-validate, or use a dedicated upgradeable mode.
sources: Brandenburg, B. and Anderson, J., 'Spin-based Reader-Writer Synchronization for Multiprocessor Real-Time Systems', Real-Time Systems, 46(1):25–87, 2010.
Mellor-Crummey, J. and Scott, M., 'Algorithms for Scalable Synchronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors', ACM TOCS, 1991.
Courtois, P., Heymans, F. and Parnas, D., 'Concurrent Control with 'Readers' and 'Writers'', Communications of the ACM, 1971.
